front: Best absorber and emitter of radiation
back: Dull (matt) black surfaces. Shiny surfaces are good reflectors and poor emitters.
Matt black inside (absorbs); insulated double walls (less conduction); glass lid (lets sunlight in, stops convection, traps infrared); foil flap (reflects extra sunlight in).

front: Why does the glass lid trap heat?
back: Sunlight passes through glass; the hot surfaces inside give out longer-wavelength infrared, much of which glass blocks. The lid also stops warm air escaping.
A shiny curved dish reflects parallel sunlight to the focus, where a black pot absorbs it. Fast and hot, but must be turned to follow the Sun; glare and burn hazard.
Box: slow (hours), about 100–150 °C, little attention needed. Curved reflector: fast, hotter, needs turning every few minutes.
Black metal absorber plate with copper pipes (good conductor), glass cover and insulation in a shallow box on the roof.
Circulation of water by convection without a pump: heated water becomes less dense and rises into the tank; cooler, denser water sinks back to the collector.

front: Where is the tank of a thermosiphon heater?
back: Above the collector. Hot water enters the top of the tank; cool water leaves from the bottom.

front: Which way do solar collectors face in Zimbabwe?
back: North, because south of the equator the midday Sun is in the northern sky for most of the year.

front: Advantages and disadvantages of solar cookers
back: For: free renewable energy, no smoke, less firewood (deforestation), lower fire risk. Against: no use at night or in cloud, slow, must face the Sun.
